```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96)
```

With competing risks, a subject can experience one of several events, and the first one that
happens prevents the others (death from another cause before relapse, for example). Two kinds of
quantities then answer different questions:

* the **cause-specific hazard** of cause $k$: the rate of cause $k$ among subjects still free of
  every event (a question about the mechanism, or aetiology);
* the **cumulative incidence** of cause $k$, $F_k(t) = P(T \le t, \text{cause} = k)$: the
  probability of having had cause $k$ by time $t$ (a question about risk, or prognosis).

A covariate can change one without changing the other, so a complete analysis reports both
(Latouche et al. 2013). SurvX has the non-parametric estimators (`aj()`, `gray_test()`), the
cause-specific hazard models (`csc()`, Cox or parametric), the Fine-Gray model (`fg()`) and the
direct parametric models of Jeong and Fine (`directcif()`).

```{r}
library(SurvX)
```

## Real data: fertility history

The `fertility` data record the time from marriage to a live birth (cause 1) or to a stillbirth
or abortion (cause 2) of 652 women in rural Shiraz (Shayan, Ayatollahi and Zare 2011).

```{r}
table(fertility$status, fertility$education)
a_f <- aj(Event(time, status) ~ education, fertility)
a_f
```

Gray's test compares the cumulative incidence of each cause across education groups. Both kinds of
model, for the main event:

```{r}
csc(Event(time, status) ~ education, fertility)          # rates of both causes
fg(Event(time, status) ~ education, fertility, cause = 1) # risk of a live birth
```

The cause-specific hazard ratios describe how fast each outcome occurs among women still waiting;
the subdistribution hazard ratio of `fg()` describes the cumulative incidence of a live birth.
The predicted cumulative incidence of a live birth for each education group, from the
cause-specific model:

```{r fert-cif, fig.height = 5}
fc <- csc(Event(time, status) ~ education, fertility)
nd <- data.frame(education = levels(fertility$education))
cif_plot(fc, newdata = nd, cause = 1, conf.int = FALSE, labels = nd$education)
```

The rest of this vignette uses simulated data, where the truth is known and every model can be
shown.

## Simulated data

We simulate 600 patients with two competing events. About a third of them never experience
either event (a cured fraction), so each CIF levels off below one. `x` is a binary covariate,
`z` a continuous one. Censoring is uniform over eight years.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
n <- 600
x <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
z <- round(runif(n, -1, 1), 2)
p1 <- plogis(-0.6 + 0.8 * x + 0.5 * z)            # probability of eventually failing from cause 1
p2 <- (1 - p1) * 0.45                             # ... from cause 2; the rest never fails
u <- runif(n)
cause <- ifelse(u < p1, 1L, ifelse(u < p1 + p2, 2L, 0L))
t_event <- ifelse(cause == 1, rweibull(n, 1.3, 2), ifelse(cause == 2, rweibull(n, 1.1, 3), Inf))
cens <- runif(n, 0, 8)
d <- data.frame(time = pmin(t_event, cens), status = ifelse(t_event <= cens, cause, 0L), x = x, z = z)
table(d$status)
```

Status 0 is censoring and 1, 2 are the two causes. Every model is specified with
`Event(time, status)` on the left-hand side of a formula.

## Non-parametric description

The Aalen–Johansen estimator gives the CIF of each cause without covariates; with a grouping
variable it also reports Gray's test.

```{r}
a <- aj(Event(time, status) ~ x, d)
a
summary(a, times = c(1, 2, 4))
```

```{r aj-plot}
plot(a)
```

Treating the competing event as censoring (one minus Kaplan–Meier) overstates the risk; compare
`km(Event(time, status == 1) ~ 1, d)` with the curve above.

## Regression models

The three approaches answer different questions.

```{r}
f_csc <- csc(Event(time, status) ~ x + z, d)   # cause-specific hazards, one Cox model per cause
f_fg  <- fg(Event(time, status) ~ x + z, d)    # Fine-Gray: subdistribution hazard of cause 1
f_dir <- directcif(Event(time, status) ~ x + z, d, baseline = "gompertz", link = "PH")
f_fg
```

`directcif()` models the CIF of **all** causes jointly. With the Gompertz baseline,
$F_k(t \mid z) = 1 - \{1 + \alpha\, e^{\beta_k^\top z} u_k(t)\}^{-1/\alpha}$ with
$u_k(t) = \tau_k (e^{\rho_k t} - 1)/\rho_k$; `link = "PH"` is $\alpha \to 0$ (proportional
subdistribution hazards), `"PO"` is $\alpha = 1$ (proportional odds) and `"GOR"` estimates
$\alpha$. When $\rho_k < 0$ the CIF levels off at a plateau, the long-run probability of cause $k$.

```{r}
summary(f_dir)
```

The link can be chosen by AIC:

```{r}
f_po  <- update(f_dir, link = "PO")
f_gor <- update(f_dir, link = "GOR")
AIC(f_dir, f_po, f_gor)
```

`estimates()` returns the coefficient table as a data frame, with exponentiated effects and
confidence limits:

```{r}
estimates(f_fg)
```

### One cause alone: the weighted estimator

The joint model needs a correct model for every cause. When only cause 1 matters,
`estimation = "weighted"` fits its direct model alone: subjects who fail from another cause enter
through the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the censoring distribution, as in Fine and Gray (1999), and
no model for the other causes is needed.

```{r}
f_w <- directcif(Event(time, status) ~ x + z, d, link = "PO", estimation = "weighted", cause = 1)
f_w
```

The censoring weights are estimated, and by default (`variance = "ipcw"`) the standard errors
account for it: the sandwich variance includes, for every subject, the effect of that subject on
the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the censoring distribution. `variance = "robust"` treats the
censoring distribution as known. The correction concerns mostly the baseline parameters, and
with them the predicted and long-run incidences; for the regression coefficients it is usually
small:

```{r}
se <- cbind(ipcw = sqrt(diag(f_w@diagnostics$vcov_ipcw)),
            censoring_known = sqrt(diag(f_w@diagnostics$vcov_robust)))
round(cbind(se, ratio = se[, 1] / se[, 2]), 4)
```

## Prediction

`predict()` gives the CIF for new covariate values at chosen times; `se = TRUE` adds
delta-method standard errors for the direct models.

```{r}
nd <- data.frame(x = c(0, 1), z = 0)
predict(f_dir, nd, times = c(1, 2, 4), cause = 1)
predict(f_fg,  nd, times = c(1, 2, 4))
predict(f_csc, nd, times = c(1, 2, 4), cause = 1)
```

`cif_plot()` draws the predicted CIFs of one or several models with confidence bands and a
risk table. Here the three models are compared for the two covariate profiles (`x = 0` and
`x = 1`, with `z = 0`). The legend names each curve by model and profile; `labels` can replace these
names, with one label per curve (here 3 models x 2 profiles = 6):

```{r cif-plot, fig.height = 5}
cif_plot(list("direct PH" = f_dir, "Fine-Gray" = f_fg, "cause-specific Cox" = f_csc),
         newdata = nd, cause = 1, B = 50)
```

The average predicted curve over the sample can be checked against the Aalen–Johansen estimate,
a quick visual test of calibration-in-the-large:

```{r cif-marginal}
cif_plot(f_dir, type = "marginal", reference = TRUE)
```

The numbers behind any plot are available with `cif_data()`, and `cif_plot(..., engine = "ggplot2")`
returns a ggplot object.

## Parametric hazard models

Giving `csc()` a parametric `baseline` fits a parametric model to the hazard of every cause
(Weibull, Gompertz, exponential, log-normal or log-logistic). The cumulative incidences are computed
from the fitted hazards, so they are coherent by construction, and they come with delta-method
confidence bands.

```{r}
f_wei <- csc(Event(time, status) ~ x + z, d, baseline = "weibull")
f_wei
AIC(f_wei, csc(Event(time, status) ~ x + z, d, baseline = "lognormal"))
```

`hazard_plot()` draws the fitted cause-specific hazards with the kernel-smoothed non-parametric
hazard (`hazard_np()`) as a reference, the visual check of the chosen distribution:

```{r hazard-plot, fig.height = 4}
hazard_plot(f_wei)
```

For a single event, `parsurv()` fits the same distributions as proportional hazards or
accelerated failure time models, with delayed entry if needed (`Event(time, status, entry = )`).
The generalized gamma (`baseline = "gengamma"`) contains the Weibull (Q = 1) and log-normal
(Q = 0) distributions, so its estimate of Q is a guide to the choice between them.

## Checking the models

`dist_plot()` shows the classic linearising plots of the non-parametric cumulative hazard: the
distribution whose panel gives straight lines is a good candidate. Given a fitted model it draws the
Cox-Snell residual plot instead, which follows the diagonal when the model fits.

```{r dist-plot, fig.height = 6}
dist_plot(Event(time, status) ~ x, d, cause = 1)
```

`ph_test()` tests proportional hazards for every covariate of a Cox or cause-specific Cox model
(the score test of Grambsch and Therneau, as in `survival::cox.zph`); `plot()` shows how the effect
changes over time. `residuals()` gives martingale, deviance, Cox-Snell and Schoenfeld residuals.

```{r ph-test, fig.height = 3.5}
pt <- ph_test(f_csc)
pt
plot(pt, cause = 1)
```

`time_effects()` goes one step further: for every covariate that fails the test it compares forms of
the change (log-linear, a step, a spline in log time), refits the model with the chosen forms and
reports the hazard ratio over time. It works on cause-specific Cox models (one analysis per cause) and
on Fine-Gray models, where the effect is a time-varying subdistribution hazard ratio.

```{r time-effects}
time_effects(f_csc)
time_effects(fg(Event(time, status) ~ education, fertility, cause = 1))
```

## Comparing the models

`compare_models()` fits a default set of direct models together with Fine–Gray and cause-specific
Cox, and scores them by the Brier score, the index of prediction accuracy (IPA), the time-dependent
AUC and the calibration error, both in the data (apparent) and by K-fold cross-validation.

```{r compare}
cm <- compare_models(Event(time, status) ~ x + z, d, times = c(1, 2, 4), folds = 3)
cm
```

```{r compare-plot}
plot(cm, measure = "ipa")
```

For a list of your own models use `cv_compare()`; the individual measures are also available as
`brier_score()`, `auc_t()` and `calibration()`.

### Scanning all models at once

`model_scan()` fits every model of the package that suits the data (here the cause-specific Cox
and parametric models, Fine-Gray and the direct models), compares them on the cross-validated
integrated Brier score, and groups together the models that predict equally well (within one
standard error of the best, a paired comparison on the same folds). AIC is shown only among the
models with a full likelihood of the same data, and every model is checked (proportional hazards,
incidences that add up to more than one, distance from the Aalen-Johansen estimate):

```{r scan}
sc <- model_scan(Event(time, status) ~ x + z, d, cause = 1, depth = "quick", folds = 3)
sc
```

```{r scan-plot, fig.height = 7}
plot(sc)
```

`report(sc, file = "scan.html")` writes a complete HTML report with the tables, the figures, a
methods paragraph and the references.

## Adjusted cumulative incidence

`adjusted_risk()` turns a model into absolute risks standardised over the covariates: the cumulative
incidence that would have been seen had every woman had a given level of education. With competing
risks the contrast is a total effect on the cumulative incidence.

```{r adjusted-risk}
adjusted_risk(fg(Event(time, status) ~ education, data = fertility, cause = 1), fertility, "education",
              times = c(1, 2, 5), B = 0)
```

## Interval-censored competing risks

When the event and its type are found at a visit, the time is known only to lie between two
visits. With `Interval(left, right, cause = )` the joint likelihood of the direct model uses
$F_k(R) - F_k(L)$ for an event of cause $k$ between the visits and $1 - \sum_k F_k(L)$ for a
subject event-free at the last visit $L$ (Hudgens, Satten and Longini 2001):

```{r ic-cr}
v <- 0.5                                      # visits every half time unit
dic <- d
dic$right <- ifelse(d$status > 0, ceiling(d$time / v) * v, Inf)   # first visit after the event
dic$left  <- ifelse(d$status > 0, dic$right - v, d$time)          # the visit before it
f_ic <- directcif(Interval(left, right, cause = status) ~ x + z, data = dic, baseline = "gompertz", link = "PH")
cbind(interval = coef(f_ic), exact = coef(f_dir))
```

The estimates from the visit data are close to those from the exact times; treating the visit at
which the event was found as the event time would shift the curves to the right.

## Coherence: do the CIFs add up?

The CIFs of all causes must sum to at most one. The cause-specific Cox approach satisfies this
by construction. Fine–Gray models fitted separately for each cause, and direct models fitted cause
by cause, do not. The joint likelihood of the direct model ties the causes together through the
event-free patients, but only if some patients remain event-free: when (almost) every subject
eventually experiences one of the events, the plateaus are not identified and the fitted CIFs can
add up to far more than one. Always check the sum before reporting predictions for several causes:

```{r}
tt <- c(1, 2, 4, 8)
s_dir <- predict(f_dir, d, times = tt, cause = 1) + predict(f_dir, d, times = tt, cause = 2)
f_fg2 <- fg(Event(time, status) ~ x + z, d, cause = 2)
s_fg  <- predict(f_fg, d, times = tt) + predict(f_fg2, d, times = tt)
c(direct = max(s_dir), "Fine-Gray" = max(s_fg))
```

When every subject eventually fails from one of the causes, `directcif(..., estimation =
"constrained")` makes the long-run incidences add up to one by construction. With two causes this
is the model of Shi, Cheng and Jeong (2013): the cause of interest has its direct model with a
plateau $F_1(\infty \mid z)$, and the other cause takes the rest,
$F_2(t \mid z) = \{1 - F_1(\infty \mid z)\}\, G(t)$. With three or more causes the rest is
shared among the competing causes by a multinomial logit in the covariates,
$F_k(t \mid z) = \{1 - F_1(\infty \mid z)\}\, \pi_k(z)\, G_k(t)$, in the manner of the
mixture model of Larson and Dinse (1985):

```{r}
d3 <- d
set.seed(5)
d3$status[d3$status == 2 & runif(nrow(d3)) < 0.4] <- 3      # split cause 2 into two causes
f_k3 <- directcif(Event(time, status) ~ x + z, d3, estimation = "constrained", cause = 1, cond = "weibull")
f_k3
```

The `share_` coefficients of cause 3 are log odds ratios of failing from cause 3 rather than from
cause 2, among the subjects who do not fail from cause 1. The long-run incidences add up to one
for every covariate value:

```{r}
nd <- data.frame(x = 0:1, z = 0)
rowSums(sapply(1:3, function(k) predict(f_k3, nd, times = Inf, cause = k)))
```

  risk. *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 94, 496-509.
